Interesting stuff. Well, the main problem with lumping anything into barbarian or savage culture from an anthropological viewpoint is it does not pinpoint the different socio-cultural apparatuses, ways of life, and the more refined mechanics that defined a particular culture.

You only get a glimpse from the material culture that you are able to find. Trying to piece the whole puzzle together is very, very interpretative and ends up in either a kind of anachronistic thinking or trying to project back from a modern point of view.

This sort of leaves open the question of we just don't know at times, but can only figure out the outer linings and work back from that point. For instance, in the future do you think telling from our religious views/symbolism and social structures/system we were necessarily an advanced culture, just on the basis of finding a few things here and there. Of course, more biodegradable things, especially the highly advanced technological tools and machines would possibly be lost, but someone might only see something more trivial and say well I guess they were not that advanced. Of course, there is the capacity to look at it from another angle. The quality of certain material culture, like flint designs, pottery designs, and generally art works/musical instruments/sometimes crude tools used for medical purposes can shine light on how advanced a culture is in some base form.

It can never shine a lot on the mechanics working behind the scene(the chemical component) that made one culture, with the limited or limitless amount of resources they had, more advanced. There are a lot of complexities involved in what defines the evolution of civilization and I would even go so far to say there is not exactly a clear cut correlation between what anthropology considers advanced civilization and the intangibles of the mind that make for an advanced modern civilization.
